tips: Read it in three movements: entering the land (chapters 1–5), taking it (6–12), and dividing it among the tribes (13–21). The long boundary lists show God keeping his promise to Abraham in concrete, mappable detail.
Watch how victory depends on faithfulness rather than strength. Jericho falls by obedience (chapter 6), while Israel loses at little Ai because of Achan's hidden sin (chapter 7).
Notice the outsiders who join Israel—Rahab of Jericho (chapter 2) and the Gibeonites (chapter 9). The book's warfare is set alongside surprising mercy.

looksBack.title: Moses' successor
looksBack.text: Joshua opens right after Moses' death (Deuteronomy 34:5–9), and God's words to Joshua repeat Moses' charge: "be strong and of a good courage" (Joshua 1:6; Deuteronomy 31:7).

looksBack.title: The promise kept
looksBack.text: The land given to Israel fulfills God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:18–21); Joshua concludes that "there failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken" (Joshua 21:45).

looksAhead.title: Unfinished conquest
looksAhead.text: The land not yet taken (Joshua 13:1–7) and Joshua's warnings against the nations that remain (Joshua 23:12–13) set up the troubles of Judges 1–2.

looksAhead.title: A greater rest
looksAhead.text: Hebrews says that if Joshua had given Israel final rest, God would not have spoken of another day; "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God" (Hebrews 4:8–9).

tips: Learn the cycle introduced in Judges 2:11–19: Israel does evil, God gives them into enemy hands, they cry out, God raises a judge, and the land has rest—until the judge dies. Each story repeats it, but the cycle spirals downward.

Don't assume every judge is a hero. Gideon ends by making a golden ephod that Israel worships (Judges 8:27), Jephthah makes a rash vow, and Samson breaks nearly every rule of his calling. The book often reports wrongdoing without comment and lets the reader judge.

Read chapters 17–21 as the book's conclusion, not an appendix. Their refrain, "In those days there was no king in Israel" (Judges 21:25), explains the moral chaos and points toward the need for faithful leadership.

looksBack.title: After Joshua
looksBack.text: Judges begins with Joshua's death (Judges 1:1; 2:8) and a generation "which knew not the LORD" (Judges 2:10), showing the warnings of Joshua 23 coming true.

looksAhead.title: The call for a king
looksAhead.text: The refrain that Israel had no king leads directly into 1 Samuel, where the people ask Samuel to "make us a king to judge us like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5).

looksAhead.title: Heroes of faith
looksAhead.text: Despite their flaws, Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah are named among the faithful in Hebrews 11:32–34.

tips: Read it against its setting: "in the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1). After the violence of Judges, this quiet story shows faithfulness surviving in ordinary families.
Watch for the Hebrew idea of kindness and loyal love. Ruth shows it to Naomi, Boaz shows it to Ruth, and through them God's own care for Naomi becomes visible.
Learn what a kinsman-redeemer is (Leviticus 25:25; Deuteronomy 25:5–6). Boaz's willingness to redeem Naomi's land and marry Ruth is the turning point of chapters 3–4.

looksBack.title: A Moabite joins Israel
looksBack.text: Moab was descended from Lot (Genesis 19:36–37) and had been barred from Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), which makes Ruth's welcome among God's people all the more striking.

looksAhead.title: Great-grandmother of David
looksAhead.text: The book ends with a genealogy leading to David (Ruth 4:17–22), making it a bridge from the judges to Israel's greatest king in 1 and 2 Samuel.

looksAhead.title: In the line of Jesus
looksAhead.text: Ruth and Boaz are named in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5–6), one of several women from outside Israel in that list.

tips: Follow three main characters in turn: Samuel, the last judge (chapters 1–7); Saul, the first king (8–15); and David, the king God chooses (16–31). The story is about what kind of leader God wants.

Watch the contrast between Saul and David. Saul looks impressive but fails to obey; David is overlooked but is a man after God's own heart. "The LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7) is the key to the book.
Read Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 2:1–10) as the book's theme song: God brings low and lifts up. The rest of 1 Samuel acts it out.

looksBack.title: The end of the judges
looksBack.text: Samuel's birth comes when Israel had "no king" and the priesthood was corrupt (1 Samuel 2:12–17), continuing the decline traced in Judges.

looksAhead.title: Hannah's song and Mary's
looksAhead.text: Mary's song at Jesus' coming (Luke 1:46–55) closely echoes Hannah's prayer, celebrating God who "hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Luke 1:52).

looksAhead.title: David's rise
looksAhead.text: David's anointing (1 Samuel 16:13) begins the line of kings that 2 Samuel continues and the New Testament traces to Jesus, "the son of David" (Matthew 1:1).

tips: Read it in two halves: David's rise to power and blessing (chapters 1–10), then his sin with Bathsheba and its long consequences in his own family (11–24).
Treat chapter 7 as the center of the book. God's covenant with David—that his throne will be established forever—shapes the hope of the rest of the Bible.
Notice how honestly David is portrayed. His adultery and murder are not hidden, but neither is his repentance (2 Samuel 12:13); Psalm 51 is traditionally linked to this moment.

looksBack.title: After Saul
looksBack.text: 2 Samuel begins with news of Saul's death on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31; 2 Samuel 1:1–12), and David's lament for Saul and Jonathan.

looksAhead.title: The covenant with David
looksAhead.text: God's promise of an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16) is echoed by the prophets (Isaiah 9:6–7) and announced as fulfilled in Jesus: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32).

looksAhead.title: Solomon's succession
looksAhead.text: The question of which son will follow David runs through 2 Samuel and is settled in 1 Kings 1–2.

tips: Track the book's great turning point: Solomon's glory (chapters 1–10), his turn to other gods (11), and the kingdom splitting in two (12). Everything after follows two kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah in the south.

Notice how each king is judged by one standard—whether he did right in the sight of the LORD like David, or followed the sins of Jeroboam. The writer cares about faithfulness more than political success.
Read the Elijah stories (chapters 17–19) as the book's spiritual climax: one prophet confronts King Ahab, Queen Jezebel, and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.

looksBack.title: David's last days
looksBack.text: 1 Kings opens with the aged David and the struggle to succeed him, continuing the family troubles of 2 Samuel.

looksBack.title: Deuteronomy's warnings
looksBack.text: Solomon's many wives, horses, and gold (1 Kings 10:26–11:4) break the law for kings in Deuteronomy 17:16–17, and the kingdom divides as a result.

looksAhead.title: Elijah's return
looksAhead.text: Malachi 4:5 promises Elijah will come again, and Jesus identifies John the Baptist with that hope (Matthew 11:14); Elijah also appears with Jesus at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3).

looksAhead.title: Something greater than Solomon
looksAhead.text: Jesus points to the queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon (1 Kings 10:1–10) and says "a greater than Solomon is here" (Matthew 12:42).

tips: Keep a list of kings as you read; the story alternates between the northern kingdom (Israel) and the southern kingdom (Judah). Each king's introduction dates his reign by the king ruling in the other kingdom, which helps you keep the two in step.
Read chapter 17 slowly. It explains why the northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and the explanation is spiritual: they "feared other gods" and would not listen to the prophets.
Notice the hopeful notes even in judgment—the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, and the final scene of King Jehoiachin released from prison (2 Kings 25:27–30), a hint that David's line has not ended.

looksBack.title: Elijah to Elisha
looksBack.text: 2 Kings continues directly from 1 Kings; Elijah is taken up into heaven and Elisha receives his spirit (2 Kings 2:9–15).

looksAhead.title: Exile and the prophets
looksAhead.text: The fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25) is the background of Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, and Daniel, and the return from exile is told in Ezra and Nehemiah.

looksAhead.title: Elisha and Naaman
looksAhead.text: Jesus cites the healing of the Syrian commander Naaman (2 Kings 5) as an example of God's mercy reaching outsiders (Luke 4:27).
